articles.title: ‘A Bit of Light’ Review: A Life-Affirming Drama About a Suicidal Iranian Doctor
articles.summary: Although its story unspools on the precipice of the U.S.-Iran war, Ali Asgari’s gentle family drama “A Bit of Light” was filmed in the conflict’s wake, under shellfire in Tehran.
body: Ali Asgari’s Venice competition entry threads a needle between morose humor and gentle naturalism.

Every interaction becomes a hurdle for Arash, if only because the imperfections of life in modern Iran reinforce the sensation of being truly alive, in all its rankling complexity. Asgari highlights these minor skirmishes through life itself (whether at its most verbose, or in complete silence) via minor aesthetic transformations which play in major keys, and prove deeply moving. The film by and large follows the edicts of Iranian neorealism, with unobtrusive observations and a naturalistic soundscape.

However, in moments entirely unexpected, the director smuggles hints of expressionism into his diegesis, crafted delicately with cinematographer and editor Iman Tahsin — like when Arash visits Mahsa’s yoga studio, and becomes captivated by her echoing instructions. He’s taken by the meditative musical vibrations, and he’s even framed against a glass window that appears to shimmer, as though the rusty gears of his mind and heart are forced to rotate and a power a bulb somewhere off screen.

articles.title: Venice Days Winners: Argentinian Director Maria Aparicio’s ‘Sadness Sometimes, Sometimes Rebellion’ Claims Top Prize
articles.summary: Argentinian director Maria Aparicio’s drama “Sometimes Sadness, Sometimes Rebellion” — which mixes personal and political elements — has scored the Venice Days director’s award, the section’s top prize.
body: The jury, headed by Spanish filmmaker Carla Simón, said in a statement: “A woman. A man. Encounters and missed encounters. A possible love story. Two great actors. A film that portrays the solitude of the present, holding together an intimate dimension and a political charge, inviting us to think about labor, immigration and privilege through a delicate mise en scène built on small gestures rather than big events.”

The statement continued, “The personal and the collective, fiction and documentary, history and present time merge into a single breath. We left the cinema deeply moved, by a sadness and a spirit of rebellion that do not oppose one another, but coexist, as two faces of the same disorientation.”
The section’s top award comes with a cash prize of €20,000 ($23,000). This is to be split equally between the filmmaker and the film’s international distributor, which is Spain’s Paper Moon.
“Sometimes Sadness, Sometimes Rebellion” is lead produced by Argentina’s La Buena Hora Cine.

articles.title: ‘Danny Boyle, please make another film about drugs’: Venice film festival’s feedback wall takes no prisoners
articles.summary: The written forum allows members of the public to vent their fury at the movies they’ve seen – and the festival organisers. In an industry that is reliant on the fickle vagaries of taste, film festivals exist to establish facts.
body: Film festivals, in turn, need beautiful A-listers to attract coverage and sponsorship, and hence there is a constant risk that these annual events become gigantic hype machines, in which every turkey is a classic and every half-hearted performance a masterclass.

Which is why there may not be a more important institution in world cinema than the Venice film festival’s Ridateci i soldi (“Give us our money back”): a makeshift chipboard wall erected next to the Palazzo del Cinema on which visitors are encouraged – with the blessing of the management – to scribble complaints and hatchet jobs in the most scathing terms possible.

The wall’s 30-year tradition commands that the festival’s director Alberto Barbera has to personally hand out a prize to the meanest diatribe, making Venice’s wall of shame a barrier against hype, an institutionalised pricking of the film world’s own pomposity.

On the Lido this year, there were complaints about the rising cost of entry badges, water taxis and local accommodation (“Maybe by 2030 we’ll have to pay for the oxygen we breathe”), queue lengths, uncomfortable seats and ceiling lights going on in the screening rooms.

articles.title: Being Heumann review – Coda director’s disability rights drama is well-intentioned but clunky
articles.summary: Toronto film festival: the rousing story of Judith Heumann makes for obvious dramatic fodder and at times this biopic finds a rebellious groove but too much feels cut-and-paste.
body: O n my way to Toronto, I wheeled my suitcase toward the taxi that would take me to the airport, finding the curb cut in the sidewalk so that my luggage could roll seamlessly down to the street. What a nice convenience provided by municipal governments all over the United States, one that so many of us take wholly for granted.

Being Heumann is Heder’s follow-up to the Oscar-winning Coda, a film about a mixed family of deaf and hearing people significant in film history for centering disability so prominently and being handsomely rewarded for it. That is a woefully rare occurrence in Hollywood, though Coda (and its contemporary, Sound of Metal ) has had a noticeable impact on deaf representation on screen in the years since. Heder would thus seem the ideal steward for another film highlighting the lives and passions of physically marginalized people, who for so terribly long were essentially cut off from the rest of society because they lacked safe, proper access to public spaces.

articles.title: Museum agrees to return remains to ancestral homeland
articles.summary: Oxford's Pitt Rivers Museum will return more than three dozen sets of human remains to the Naga people.
body: More than three dozen sets of human remains taken during the British colonial rule of India and Myanmar are set to be returned to their ancestral home by a museum.
Skulls and bones belonging to the Naga people of northeastern India and Myanmar - formerly known as Burma - have been displayed at the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford for more than a century.
In 2020, the museum removed all human remains from public display as part of what the it called a "decolonisation process" - including the ancestral Naga remains.
The museum has now announced that a formal decision has been made by the University of Oxford Council to return the 39 ancestral human remains to their homeland.

articles.title: ‘People think fame is a magic wand’: Jarvis Cocker on old songs, young fans and his granny’s verdict on Pulp
articles.summary: Before the release of a joyful film on the history of the Sheffield band, frontman Cocker and director Garth Jennings talk dark times, taking inspiration from Abba – and why there could yet be another record.
body: When the director Garth Jennings first moved to Paris, Jarvis Cocker, who was living there, dropped in on his old friend. “And I nearly got you arrested,” the Pulp frontman recalls. It was bonfire night, and Cocker had taken some welcoming fireworks over to Jennings’ place. “It turned out Garth’s apartment was quite near to the – not an army base, but what’s it called?”
“So obviously they didn’t like explosives,” says Cocker. “We got told off for that. The best welcome to Paris.”

The men had first met in the late 1990s, when Jennings directed two gorgeous music videos for Pulp, for the singles Help the Aged and A Little Soul. Now, almost 30 years later, they are working together again, on Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore? This joyful, funny, celebratory film is a hybrid beast: part concert movie and part documentary on the long history of the band. The live show was filmed at London’s O2 Arena in the summer of 2025, on the night that Pulp were told that More, their eighth studio album and first album in 24 years, had gone to No 1 in the British album charts. You can see Cocker waving around the trophy on stage.

articles.title: James Bay performs with broken ankle at Bon Jovi gig
articles.summary: The Hitchin-born star is wheeled onto the stage with his leg in a cast for his set at Wembley.
body: James Bay came on stage in a wheelchair to support Bon Jovi at Wembley Stadium on Wednesday.
The Brit Award-winning singer-songwriter, born in Hitchin, Hertfordshire, had broken his ankle the day before.
The 36-year-old had to perform while sitting down, with his left leg and ankle in a cast.
In a caption on Instagram, the venue said the star had broken "his ankle on Tuesday... but still supported Bon Jovi on Wednesday".

articles.summary: Elsewhere, the Europa Cinemas Label has gone to Robert Guediguian's 'A Woman Today,' and Nicola Sorcinelli's 'Balcanica' stormed the People's Choice Award.
body: With this year’s Venice Film Festival drawing to a close, the dishing out of awards has begun.

“A film that portrays the solitude of the present, holding together an intimate dimension and a political charge, inviting us to think about labor, immigration and privilege through a delicate mise en scène built on small gestures rather than big events,” said the jury, which also included Italian director Sara Fgaier and editor Hania Mroué. “We left the cinema deeply moved, by a sadness and a spirit of rebellion that do not oppose one another, but coexist, as two faces of the same disorientation.”

Elsewhere, the Europa Cinemas Label, instituted by a network of European exhibitors with the support of the EU’s MEDIA program, is dedicated to European films and co-productions. articles.title: ‘Ancestors’ Invites You to a Cinematic “Séance,” Led by Éanna Hardwicke, That Mixes Dream, Reality and Memory (Exclusive TIFF Clip and Chat)
articles.summary: Jack Wolfe, Jessica Reynolds, Christina Hendricks and Rupert Everett also feature in David Turpin's feature directorial debut, the poster for which we can also reveal ahead of its world premiere at Toronto.
body: Is Ancestors, the directorial feature debut of The Lodgers and The Winter Lake writer David Turpin, a love story, a noir mystery or a metaphysical fable? Well, it is all of the above – and more!
Ancestors will world-premiere in the Discovery program of the Toronto International Film Festival ( TIFF ) on Saturday, Sept. 12.

Ancestors follows the charismatic but vulnerable Beau, portrayed by Hardwicke, as he searches across 1980s London for his missing friend Tiny, played by Wolfe. A haunting journey awaits the Irishman abroad at a time when homosexuality was still illegal in his homeland. “Dream, reality, memory and history entwine, ultimately bringing Beau face-to-face with life, death and the beyond,” teases a synopsis for the film. All these elements “come together on the edge of morality — where he discovers the truth about Tiny, and about himself.”
Ancestors features cinematography by Patrick Jordan and editing by Stephanie McCutcheon. Mister Smith Entertainment is handling sales. THR can debut the poster for the film right here.
